Amazon announces water replenishment project in Germany, expected to return more than 750 million liters annually
Amazon has announced a water replenishment project with Microsoft in Hesse, 
Germany
. The project will restore natural wetland conditions across 40 hectares in the Vogelsberg region, a critical water sourcing area that supplies a significant portion of Frankfurt's drinking water.
NABU, Germany's oldest and largest environmental association, is implementing the project with funding from both companies. Supported by Amazon's contribution of over €2.9 million, the project is expected to return more than 750 million liters of water annually to the local groundwater supply once completed, helping replenish water resources for the city and its surrounding communities.
Amazon invests $20 million in the Colorado River as part of a coalition to mobilize $100 million for water conservation 
Amazon is launching a collaborative action initiative alongside other companies to fund water projects across the basin.
The project marks Amazon's third water replenishment initiative in Germany, following the urban leak detection program in Frankfurt and the wetland restoration in the Spessart Forest. Together, Amazon's contributions to these three projects are expected to return more than 920 million liters of water annually.
Nature-based groundwater recharge in the Vogelsberg
Working with local landholders, NABU will gradually acquire a total of 80 hectares of land from 2026 onwards, with further acquisitions planned through the end of 2028. The project will restore wetland conditions across 40 hectares of land through proven nature-based approaches: removing artificial drainage systems, creating shallow water zones and depressions that slow water flow and increase infiltration, and establishing extensive grassland management to reduce nutrient inputs into streams. The work will be carried out in collaboration with the city of Herbstein and local farmers.
Delivering biodiversity benefits alongside water resilience
The project is also expected to create habitats for species that have declined significantly in the region, including whinchats, snipe, wood sandpipers, and gadwall. The region's cooler climate also makes it a potential refuge for species displaced by warming in surrounding lowlands—positive effects already demonstrated by comparable NABU projects in the area. Biodiversity impact will be measured through annual monitoring of mammals, birds, insects, amphibians, and reptiles between 2028 and 2038—ensuring over a decade of evidence on the project's ecological outcomes.

Amazon's forest replenishment projects in Japan expected to return 300 million liters of water per year to communities
Amazon has announced its newest water replenishment project in 
Japan
, a forest restoration initiative in Chiba prefecture.
Carried out in collaboration with the Chiba Prefecture Forestry Association, the work centers on tree thinning: a practice that restores the forest's ability to retain water and supports healthier water flows upstream of the Yoro River. This is the water source that supplies communities in the region where we operate. The restoration efforts will cover 250 hectares of forest in total, and once complete, are expected to return more than 170 million liters of water per year back to local communities.
"Japan's forests face growing pressures from aging tree populations and changing climate conditions. The work we do—thinning, clearing, restoring—is essential to keeping our watersheds healthy and our water supply dependable," said Yoshikazu Yamamoto, director and president of the Chiba Prefectural Forestry Association. "Amazon's investment allows us to do more of this work, faster, in the areas where it matters most. When forests thrive, water flows, and that benefits everyone downstream."
Water is one of Japan's most vital natural resources—sustaining communities, agriculture, and ecosystems across the country. As Amazon, through 
Amazon Web Services (AWS)
, continues to grow its cloud infrastructure in Japan, we are investing in efficient 
data center
 cooling technologies and community water replenishment projects to protect the water resources that communities depend on.
Amazon announced its first water replenishment project in Japan in 2025. The project involves the maintenance of the forests in Tabayama Village, Yamanashi. Maintenance activities include thinning, pruning, and managing young tree growth to reduce competition among trees. This allows more water to infiltrate the soil, replenishing groundwater and increasing water availability. The ongoing project is on track to return over 130 million liters of water each year to the local community once completed.

AWS now replenishes more water than it uses in data centers in Aragón, Spain; launches project set to save 10 billion liters annually
Amazon Web Services
 (AWS) has confirmed it is currently replenishing more water than it uses across its direct data center operations in Aragón, 
Spain
. It also announced a new water recovery project set to save more than 10 billion liters annually once completed.
As of today, AWS's projects are already giving back more than 1 billion liters of water a year to the community with two of its water projects, focused on smarter crop watering and the reuse of leftover irrigation water through a natural solution. As a result, the company is already putting back more water than it uses in its 
data centers
 in Aragón. In practical terms, for every one liter AWS needs to run its data centers in Aragón, around 15 liters are returned to the local water system through these projects. 
AWS made these announcements during the second edition of TECH4WATER.
"I am very proud to say that in Aragón we are already returning more water than we use in our local data centers. Behind this milestone is an extraordinary team that works and innovates every day to make our data sites more efficient," says Paul Meaney, director of data center operations for AWS in Europe, the Middle East and Africa.
Through several local water projects, AWS is investing in making the entire region and its communities better prepared to handle water challenges—upgrading aging water systems, improving how water is delivered to homes and farms, and helping the area better cope with the effects of climate change. 
A new project to save over 10 billion liters of water every year
Working alongside Comunidad General de Usuarios del Canal Imperial de Aragón, and with technical support from local tech partner Agrow Analytics, this new project aims to replace 25 kilometers of open ground irrigation ditches with enclosed pipes—cutting down on water lost to evaporation and leaks.
The project will also place sensors in the ground to measure soil moisture, use satellite images to understand exactly how much water crops need, and develop smart technology that predicts the best times and amounts to water. With a total investment of €3.73 million for this specific initiative, the goal is to save more than 10 billion liters of water every year once the project is fully completed by 2030.

Amazon to deploy water conservation project in India, replenishing an estimated 178 million liters annually once completed
Amazon today announced a collaboration with 
FluxGen
, a water technology start-up, to deploy an integrated water conservation project at the National Chemical Laboratory (NCL) research campus in Pune, 
India
.
The project, spanning the 380-acre campus, is expected to replenish an estimated 178 million liters of water annually once completed by end of this year. It will use smart sensors and efficient fixtures including aerators and waterless urinals to reduce consumption, capture and recycle wastewater, and recharge groundwater across the campus.
The collaboration is part of Amazon’s wider water stewardship efforts in India, 
where the company recently achieved its goal of becoming water positive
—returning 120% of the water it uses across its direct operations to communities and the environment—ahead of its 2027 target.
Amazon teams up with leading Indian university to turn farm waste into recyclable packaging
The collaboration with the Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee will reduce plastic usage and cut air pollution.
"This collaboration with FluxGen reflects our deep commitment to water stewardship in India. The NCL campus in Pune is an ideal setting to demonstrate how technology-driven interventions can make a real difference at scale," said Karan Chugh, director of operations for Amazon India. "By investing in integrated water management solutions here, we’re not just addressing local water challenges—we’re building a model that can be replicated across offices, commercial spaces, schools, hospitals, multi-unit housing, and institutional campuses nationwide."
The project also encompasses an experiential learning initiative, scheduled to launch in 2027, aimed at building awareness of water conservation among young people. The programme will include quarterly student visits to the NCL campus for hands-on exposure to water management technologies, the establishment of water conservation clubs in local schools, and the introduction of “HydroQuest”—an educational board game that teaches water conservation principles.

Amazon invests nearly $1 million to restore wetlands and wildlife habitat along Ohio’s Scioto River
Early stages of wetland restoration at the Glacier Ridge project.
Amazon is investing nearly $1 million to restore wetlands and grasslands across 66 acres in central 
Ohio
—work that is expected to filter and improve the quality of more than 72 million gallons of water annually in the Scioto River.
In collaboration with the 
Ohio Department of Natural Resources
 and the 
Columbus and Franklin County Metro Parks
, work will take place at two sites: Prairie Oaks Metro Park in Hilliard and Glacier Ridge Metro Park in Plain City.
At Prairie Oaks, the project will create and enhance 18 acres of wetland habitat. This includes dense grass meadows that act as natural filers, slowing water down so soil can absorb nutrients before they reach nearby waterways. It also includes shallow seasonal pools that fill with rain and snowmelt each spring, providing breeding habitat for wildlife that depend on these temporary water sources. Together, these restored areas will help catch fertilizers and other excess nutrients that wash off surrounding land. In waterways, too many nutrients can fuel algae blooms that harm fish and degrade drinking water. The project is designed to reduce that risk in the Darby Creek watershed, a tributary of the Scioto River.
At Glacier Ridge, the project will restore 45 acres of grassland, create three acres of shallow seasonal pools, and plant new trees—all of which will help absorb and filter stormwater runoff from nearby development before it reaches the Scioto River, protecting water quality over time.
Beyond water quality, the restored grasslands, wetlands, and seasonal pools will provide nesting and foraging habitat for declining grassland bird species, including Henslow's sparrows, savanna sparrows, bobolinks, eastern and western meadowlarks, and upland sandpipers, as well as other wildlife such as red foxes, coyotes, eastern cottontails, and black racers. Work is expected to be completed in 2027.
In 2025, 
Amazon data centers
 in Ohio withdrew approximately 93 million gallons of water—about the same volume that flows past downtown Columbus in the Scioto River in just over two hours. The company’s Ohio data centers operate at a water use effectiveness (WUE) of 0.06 L/kWh—more than nine times better than the U.S. data center industry average. To date, Amazon has cumulatively contracted projects for Ohio watersheds that replenish 97 million gallons of clean water per year.

Amazon expands water replenishment programs in Brazil, recovering an additional 785 million liters annually
Amazon has announced two new water supply initiatives in 
Brazil
.
The first will bring more efficiency to crop irrigation, contributing to water security in the metropolitan region of Belo Horizonte by saving 200 million liters annually once completed. In São Paulo, the objective is to detect leaks in water supply systems to avoid wasting 585 million liters of water once finalized.
Both initiatives were announced at the 
AWS
 Summit São Paulo.
Tackling water stress with smart irrigation technology
In a first-of-its-kind collaboration with agritech firm Phytech, Amazon will fully fund a project to monitor plant health and soil moisture on more than 390 hectares (970 acres) of farmland using 
Artificial Intelligence
 (AI) hosted on the AWS cloud. The technology, which consists of sensors installed on the plants, will allow local farmers to match irrigation with the actual needs of crops, tracking water use in real time and avoiding unneeded watering.
01

The intervention will focus on the basins of the Velhas and Paraopeba rivers, in Minas Gerais, which currently face severe water stress. In these basins, water demand from agriculture, industry, and municipal supply exceeds the availability of water by 60%. The initiative will help farmers reduce water withdrawal by 200 million liters annually, freeing up 2 billion liters of water over the next 10 years.
Expanding AI-powered leak detection to save nearly 800 million liters of water
Amazon also announced a significant expansion of an existing leak detection project started in 2025 in collaboration with Aganova and Sabesp, the water utility serving the São Paulo metropolitan region. This expansion will add savings of 585 million liters of water per year. Added to the original project, the total volume will jump to 795 million liters of water.
5 things to know from Amazon's 2025 Sustainability Report
As Amazon’s operations grow, so does the work behind the scenes to help make them more sustainable. Here’s where the company is making progress—and what’s ahead.
At the heart of the project is 
Aganova's Nautilus system.
 This in-line inspection technology operates inside pipelines without interrupting service. Using advanced data collection and AI-based analytics on AWS, the system can accurately detect and locate hidden leaks and air pockets — problems that conventional methods often fail to identify.

Amazon invests in Oregon irrigation upgrades expected to save more than 500 million gallons of water per year
Intake screens for the booster station. When the canal is full, they are the submerged intake for the pumps that are used to convert the acreage from flood irrigation to pressurized sprinklers.
Amazon is investing in three irrigation efficiency projects with the West Extension Irrigation District (WEID) in eastern Oregon's Umatilla and Morrow counties. Amazon's contributions to these projects will save more than 530 million gallons of water annually once completed—nearly equivalent to the amount the nearby City of Umatilla used in 2025.
The projects address water loss by upgrading open canals—channels that lose water to evaporation, seepage, and overflows—and aging measurement systems that can't track water use accurately enough to prevent waste. Real-time monitoring at key delivery points allows the district to align water diversion at the river intake to actual demand, reducing excess water that currently spills at the canal's end.
Each project provides solutions that address the water losses:
Main canal flow control:
 Eight new meters along WEID's main canal will let district operators monitor water flow in real time and divert only what’s needed, eliminating excess that currently spills unused at the canal’s end. This is expected to save 171 million gallons of water.
Canal piping and sprinkler conversion:
 More than 2.5 miles of open canal will be converted into buried pipeline, eliminating evaporation and seepage that can account for roughly 26% of the overall project savings. Additionally, 178 acres will transition from flood irrigation to pressurized sprinkler systems, delivering water directly to crop root zones and making farmers more efficient with their water use. These changes are expected to save 100 million gallons.
Customer delivery point upgrades:
 A 24-year-old metering system at customer delivery points will be replaced with modern equipment, giving WEID and its irrigators real-time visibility into usage. More accurate measurement reduces over-pumping from the Columbia River, estimated to save 260 million gallons.
Water saved will remain in the Umatilla River and Columbia River, benefiting fish habitat and reducing pumping costs for the district, which serves approximately 1,050 customers across 11,400 irrigable acres.
5 ways Amazon is investing in Oregon
Amazon's investments are boosting Oregon's economy while creating opportunities for Oregonians.
Amazon is investing alongside funding from the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation's WaterSMART program and the district's own funds, which will collectively save more than 1.2 billion gallons of water. The projects are expected to be completed in phases by March 2028.
WEID currently receives cooling water discharge from Amazon data center operations for agricultural reuse through the City of Umatilla's industrial wastewater utility, which provided more than 10 million gallons in 2025.
These projects are in addition to Amazon’s 
two other replenishment projects in the state
. Together, they contribute to Amazon's goal to replenish more water than it uses in its data center operations.

Amazon launches collaboration in Australia to restore waterways that supply Greater Sydney’s drinking water
Amazon has announced a 10-year collaboration with the 
Australian
 River Restoration Centre (ARRC), a national not-for-profit, to restore a degraded stretch of the Coxs River in Greater Western Sydney—a waterway that feeds the reservoirs supplying drinking water to millions of people.
Amazon will fund work across 14.8 kilometers of the upper Coxs River, where decades of land clearing, grazing, and invasive plant growth have eroded banks, clouded waterways with sediment, and allowed livestock waste to enter the water supply.
Once completed, the project is expected to improve water quality and availability by nearly 400 million liters of water per year for millions of people.
The two-year project will be followed by monitoring and maintenance through to 2036. It will address three interconnected challenges along the Coxs River.
Invasive willows: 
Dense willow growth has overrun creek channels, drawing large volumes of water from the system and suppressing the growth and recovery of native plants. The project will see the removal of willows and replacement with native species, helping to restore these fragile ecosystems and freeing water to flow downstream.
Erosion:
 Historic land clearing and grazing pressure have contributed to the start of active erosion, with sediment entering waterways that feed Warragamba Dam, reducing the dam's capacity to store water over time. Erosion has decreased water quality and degraded farmland and native vegetation. Erosion control programs will stabilize active erosion and increase water quality for the broader community’s benefit.
Livestock pollution:
 Unrestricted livestock access has increased nutrients and pathogens in the waterways. New livestock exclusion fencing, off-stream watering points, and dedicated crossings will help keep livestock out of waterways, reducing contaminants entering waterways and allowing bankside vegetation to regenerate as a natural filter.
The project also aims to rebuild habitat for native species including platypus, freshwater crayfish and other aquatic wildlife. Revegetation along waterways and wetlands will provide shade, stabilize banks and support the return of native plants and animals.

Amazon invests in leak-detection project in Brazil, saving up to 165 million liters of water annually
Amazon is investing to tackle water loss in Recife, Brazil, using AI-powered technology to detect hidden leaks in the city’s water system. The project is expected to save 165 million liters of water annually once completed—the equivalent of 66 Olympic swimming pools.
At the center of the effort is a system developed by Aganova, a global leader in advanced leak detection. Its Nautilus technology deploys acoustic sensors inside pipelines and uses AI-powered data analytics to accurately detect hidden leaks and air pockets.
The technology uses 
Amazon Web Services (AWS)
 to host and provide data analytics capabilities.
Recife, one of Brazil's fastest-growing coastal cities, faces increasing pressure on its water resources. Reducing physical water losses is both an operational priority and a strategic necessity: it eases extraction pressure on vulnerable water bodies and improves the efficiency of the entire distribution system.
The Nautilus system targets large-diameter transmission pipelines. While these represent a relatively small portion of the network, they account for a disproportionate share of water losses—making them a high-impact starting point for modernization.
The initiative reflects Amazon's approach to being 
a good steward of water
 in the communities where it operates. By supporting the deployment of cutting-edge detection technology, the project aims to strengthen infrastructure, preserve natural resources, and deliver lasting benefits for residents across Recife and surrounding areas.
"The collaboration between local utilities and companies applying cutting-edge technology is a smart path to solving critical city problems, such as water waste," says Juliana Sztrajtman, President of Amazon Brazil. "This initiative increases water efficiency, strengthens infrastructure, helps preserve natural resources, and provides lasting benefits for the communities of Recife and surrounding areas."

Amazon collaborates with the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation to restore forests and replenish water in Georgia
A representation of the forests that will benefit from this project in Georgia.
Amazon is investing $2 million in a new water replenishment project in Georgia through a collaboration with the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (NFWF). It is Amazon's first water replenishment project in the state, and Amazon is already funding a 
similar project
 with NFWF near Rockingham, North Carolina.
Through the project, NFWF, together with the Georgia Forest Commission, will restore 16,000 acres of longleaf pine and other open pine and oak forest within the Upper Ocmulgee watershed in the greater Atlanta, Georgia, area. The primary goal is to restore wildlife habitat and improve water flows in the region.
Activities will include invasive vegetation management to reduce vegetation cover, which in turn will benefit wildlife and reduce evapotranspiration (the amount of water absorbed by excess vegetation) and increase downstream water flows.
The project is expected to replenish an average of 370 million gallons of water annually to communities and the environment. Amazon is the sole funder of the project, which is expected to deliver benefits through December 2035.
Amazon is also investing heavily in reclaimed water infrastructure in Georgia, with 
22 reclaimed water sites
 currently under construction in collaboration with the Douglasville-Douglas County Water and Sewer Authority, Cobb County Water Systems, and the City of Covington. This means we will be using treated sewage to cool many data centers in the region instead of potable water, which is expected to save roughly 80 million gallons annually when fully operational.
This project with NFWF supports progress toward our commitment to be 
water positive globally by 2030
, returning more water to communities than we use in direct data center operations.

Amazon becomes water positive in India, returning more water to communities than it uses
Amazon today announced that it has become water positive in India, meaning the company now returns more water to communities than it uses across its direct operations, including corporate offices, data centers, and fulfillment centers across the country.
Amazon had set a goal to become water positive in 
India
 by 2027 and has now achieved it ahead of time. This milestone marks a significant step in the company's global water stewardship strategy.
India holds 18% of the global population but only 4% of global freshwater resources, making it one of the world's most water-stressed regions. Amazon responds to this reality through initiatives under three pillars:
Reduce: Improving water efficiency
Amazon-operated data centers in India do not use water for cooling. Beyond 
data centers
, water use across Amazon's other operations in India—including fulfillment centers and corporate offices—is primarily for basic human needs such as restrooms and drinking water. The company reduces water consumption through efficiency measures such as low-flow fixtures and smart water meters that monitor usage, detect leaks early, and enable rapid corrective action.
Reuse: Wastewater treatment and rainwater harvesting
As of 2025, on-site sewage treatment plants at Amazon buildings recycle wastewater, providing an estimated 298 million liters annually for toilet flushing and irrigation. Amazon is also expanding wastewater treatment capacity across its fulfillment centers to increase the reuse of treated water for applications including cleaning and cooling. In 2025, rainwater harvesting pits across Amazon facilities collected approximately 178 million liters of water, which percolates back to groundwater, replenishing local water sources.
Replenish: Investing in water-stressed communities
The company’s water replenishment efforts focus on water-stressed regions where it operates, working with local partners to strengthen water security and support surrounding communities. Amazon has committed more than $6 million towards water stewardship initiatives across the country. These projects are expected to replenish more than 4 billion liters of water annually.

Cows at one of the participating dairy farms.
Amazon is announcing two new water replenishment projects in 
Virginia
: a water quality initiative that reduces excess nutrient runoff from dairy farms with the Virginia State Dairymen's Association and Virginia Tech, and a water efficiency program with ION Water in affordable housing communities in 
.
In the first project, Amazon is funding an initiative with the Virginia State Dairymen's Association that helps Virginia dairy producers quantify and reduce nutrient runoff into local waterways through feed optimization, fertilizer reduction, and improved manure management. Participating farms receive technical support from Virginia Tech and outcome-based payments proportional to the verified nitrogen load reductions they achieve.
The project will support ongoing conservation and nutrient reduction efforts in the Potomac River and the Chesapeake Bay, protecting these vital regional watersheds for decades to come. The project expands on previous work funded by the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality and is expected to improve the quality of 500 million gallons of water per year. Implementation begins in 2026-2027 and will continue through 2035.
In the second project, Amazon is funding an initiative with ION Water to improve leak detection in five multi-unit affordable housing properties in Northern Virginia. The AWS-hosted water management system will provide property managers with data to eliminate leaks within their buildings, ultimately saving water. Implementation began in 2025 and will benefit the communities through 2035. The project is expected to conserve more than 45 million gallons of water per year.
Through these two new projects and an existing watershed restoration project with the Stroud Water Research Center that replenishes 88 million gallons of water annually, Amazon is replenishing more than 630 million gallons of water per year in Virginia. Amazon has operated 
data centers
 in Northern Virginia since 2006 and in 2025, it withdrew 263 million gallons of water in the region. These projects help Amazon make progress toward its commitment to be 
water positive by 2030
, returning more water to communities than it uses in its direct data center operations.

Amazon announces watershed restoration project in Northwest Indiana
Amazon is announcing its third water replenishment project in Northwest 
Indiana
. This project will support the restoration of approximately 425 acres of habitat along Bogus Run, a waterway feeding into the Kankakee River.
The project, implemented at Shirley Heinze Land Trust’s “Big Eastern” property, will focus on restoring native sand prairie and woodland habitats through long-term land stewardship activities. Shirley Heinze Land Trust acquired the property in May 2025, and Amazon is providing funding to restore it. Implementation is planned from 2027 through 2031 along with ongoing maintenance and monitoring in subsequent years.
Planned improvements include invasive vegetation management across approximately 325 acres, selective woodland restoration across 200 acres, and the establishment of 30 acres of native sand prairie. Together, this work is expected to improve regional water retention and availability by more than 110 million gallons annually, equivalent to the annual water usage of 1,000 U.S. households.
Over time, portions of the watershed have experienced changing drainage patterns, erosion, and habitat loss that can affect water quality and groundwater levels. By restoring native vegetation and thinning overgrown woodlands, the project is designed to help slow surface runoff, improve soil stability, and encourage more natural infiltration of water back into the ground. Native sand prairie species are particularly well-suited to Northwest Indiana’s soils and are known for their deep root systems, which help retain soil moisture, reduce erosion, and support long-term watershed resilience.
Beyond water benefits, the restoration is expected to enhance habitat for more than 1,000 species of plants, insects, reptiles, amphibians, and mammals—some of which are native species like wild lupine, black oak, sand coreopsis, and numerous sunflowers, milkweeds, and asters that showcase the importance of ongoing restoration efforts to preserving these diverse and interconnected ecosystems.
This project reflects Amazon’s aim to be a responsible water steward in the communities where it operates. It adds to a growing portfolio of more than 50 water replenishment projects globally, including two existing 
projects in Northwest Indiana
 that are expected to conserve or improve the quality of at least 100 million gallons of water each year—bringing the region's total to more than 210 million gallons annually.

Amazon launches river revitalization project in India, treating over 200 million liters annually and improving public health
Amazon has announced a ₹10 crore (US$1 million) investment for its first-ever water quality improvement project in Chennai's Adyar River watershed, expected to treat over 200 million liters annually.
The city of Chennai in India currently faces significant wastewater management challenges, with the Adyar River increasingly affected by untreated sewage, industrial effluents, and plastic waste. 
The project will feature a modular sewage treatment plant on the Buckingham Canal in Kotturpuram, a key point where untreated wastewater enters the river.  This plant will treat sewage from the canal and recycle wastewater for multiple non-drinking uses, improving public health by reducing disease outbreaks linked to untreated sewage. 
"Our country faces critical water challenges, with rivers like the Adyar suffering from severe pollution," says Abhinav Singh, vice president of operations for Amazon India and Australia. "This project will not only help restore river health but also provide the community with a valuable new source of treated water.”
The treated water will bring four distinctive benefits:
Reducing pollution and supporting river restoration
 by releasing treated water into the Adyar River
Addressing Chennai's groundwater crisis
 by channeling treated water into depleted aquifers, improving long-term water security for the region. 
Supporting the city's green spaces
 by providing irrigation for a Miyawaki forest—a dense, fast-growing woodland created using a Japanese reforestation technique—and public parks in the vicinity.
Community organizations will be able to collect treated water
 using tanker trucks for use by local schools and colleges for essential needs like toilet flushing and campus irrigation. 
The project is being implemented together with SIV Impact Inc. and in coordination with Chennai Metropolitan Water Supply and Sewerage Board, and Tamil Nadu Water Resources Department.

Amazon announces two water replenishment projects in Germany, set to save 370 million liters annually
Amazon has announced two water replenishment projects in Germany: an innovative urban leak detection initiative in Frankfurt and a wetland restoration project in the Spessart Forest upstream of the city. Together, the projects are expected to return nearly 370 million liters of water annually to the community once completed.
The projects are being carried out in collaboration with 
Shayp
, a water technology scaleup built on 
Amazon Web Services (AWS)
 cloud infrastructure, and 
EcoTree
, a European nature project developer.
Addressing urban water loss through technology
The leak detection initiative in Frankfurt tackles a critical yet often overlooked challenge: in many buildings, water leaks are not detected promptly and can account for a substantial share of total water use. Amazon is funding the installation of Shayp's smart Internet of Things (IoT) monitoring technology in 500 buildings across Frankfurt by 2028, at no cost to building owners and operators. Participating buildings, including public facilities such as schools, hospitals, and medical centers, will receive automated leak detection 24/7, enabling immediate response to water waste.
Installation of Shayp sensors will begin this year. Once installed, each sensor provides continuous 24/7 monitoring—meaning water savings start immediately and are expected to accumulate year after year, well beyond the installation period. The AWS cloud-based technology enables real-time data analysis and rapid response for detected leaks, maximizing water conservation impact from day one. Shayp will work with German facility management group 
WISAG
 to recruit participating buildings.

Amazon aims to be a good water steward everywhere it operates. For example, Amazon recently set a goal to replenish more water than we use across our India operations by 2027, and is committed to being “
water positive
” across all AWS data centers by 2030.
We’re reducing our water footprint by increasing the efficiency of our water use throughout our operations while also investing in ways to replenish water in our communities. Some examples:
Amazon is the largest corporate purchaser of renewable energy globally for the fifth year in a row
With more than 600 projects worldwide, Amazon is also supporting solar and wind initiatives in regions with polluted grids to help curb emissions.
Amazon 
scaled
 harvesting and reuse solutions in its fulfillment centers, sort centers, and delivery stations around the world. We’ve also created a global water metering and leak detection program, with one pilot in the United Kingdom saving an 
estimated 700 million liters
 of leaked water over two years.
The Boss Defrost’s powerful circulating pump system recycles meltwater instead of letting it run down the drain. Whole Foods Market stores in the Denver area with Boss Defrost systems installed saw overall store water usage decrease by an average of 12% between 2021 and 2022.
In many of its data centers AWS uses 
direct evaporative cooling and free-air cooling systems
 to remove heat from servers in data centers. Recycled water is also used for cooling at 24 data centers worldwide, preserving valuable drinking water for communities and the environment.
Amazon’s global corporate offices are increasingly using recycled water and low-flow fixtures. For example, at 
HQ2
 in Arlington, Virginia, by capturing and reusing rainwater, shower water, and HVAC condensate, the building is expected to achieve 
50% water savings below building code
, and recycle 7.5 million gallons each year.
Globally, Amazon’s 27 water replenishment projects are expected to return more than 8 billion liters of water annually once completed. These projects expand access to clean water and sanitation, improve water quality, and increase the water available to water-stressed communities. Some of these projects are already under way, while others are just commencing.
For example, earlier this month we announced three projects 
in Spain
 that are expected to reduce flood risk for 700,000 residents in the province of Zaragoza, modernize critical infrastructure, and optimize agricultural water use through artificial intelligence (AI). And in India, Amazon has invested in five projects, including partnering with the global nonprofits Water.org and WaterAid to bring clean water and sanitation to over 250,000 people surrounding our regions there.
